cards.explanation: The answer is that they want to arrest Jesus and kill Him. The chief priests and scribes want Jesus arrested and killed, and they want it done on the quiet (Mark 14:1). Covert means hidden, like trying to swipe a cookie off the cooling rack while the whole family stands right there. It never works, friends, but they're sure it will.

The word is riot. The chief priests and scribes say, “But not during the feast, or there may be a riot among the people.” (Mark 14:2) So their plan has a calendar problem. They're sneaky, but they still have to wait for the right time, like me waiting on the timer to ding before I open the oven.

The woman breaks open the jar and pours the perfume on Jesus' head. She broke open the jar and poured it on Him (Mark 14:3). Once a jar is broken open, there's no closing it back up. It's like me tipping a whole jar of sprinkles over a batch, friends, because there's no scooping them back.

The number is over three hundred denarii. The grumblers say it could have been sold for “…over three hundred denarii…” (Mark 14:5). A denarius is a coin, and three hundred of them is a big pile. I'd be checking my apron pockets for loose change just hearing that.

The word is poor. The grumblers say it could have been sold “…and the money given to the poor.” (Mark 14:5) Helping the poor is a good thing, and Jesus says so Himself in verse 7. Still, they scolded the woman over it, and that's where their talk went sideways.

Jesus says her perfume anointed His body in advance of His burial. He says, “She has done what she could to anoint My body in advance of My burial.” (Mark 14:8) She poured out the perfume, and Jesus told them what it meant. Burial is the word He uses.

What she did will be told in memory of her. Jesus says, “And truly I tell you, wherever the gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” (Mark 14:9) I want my cookies remembered, and she gets the whole world. That's a lot of retelling, friends.

The one who goes to the chief priests is Judas Iscariot. He is one of the Twelve, and he went to the chief priests to betray Jesus (Mark 14:10). This is one of the heavy parts of the story, so I'll just say that plainly. I think it's a hard line to read.

The two answers are delighted and money. “They were delighted to hear this, and they promised to give him money.” (Mark 14:11) The chief priests had been searching for a covert way, and then one of the Twelve walked right up to them. I think that's a hard thing to read, so I'll say it plainly.
